title: Start · What this book is about
intro: Meet Jurgen Appelo's «Agile Management»: who it is for, why «Management 3.0», and the three types of people in the leadership debate. (English, B1–B2.)

steps.title: The book and the author
steps.body:
Jurgen Appelo is a Dutch manager and software developer. For about ten years he led development teams — as a team leader, a project manager and finally as CIO of one of the biggest e-commerce companies in the Netherlands. In parallel he was reading books about complexity theory: chaos, networks, self-organisation.

At some point the two things clicked together. He saw that agile software development is, in fact, complexity theory in practice, and that a software team is a perfect example of a complex adaptive system: many people, many connections, and results that nobody can fully predict.

There was one problem. There were dozens of books about agile methods for developers, testers, coaches and project managers — and almost nothing for team leaders and managers. So he started a blog (noop.nl) in 2008 to test his ideas with readers. In 18 months he had 4000 subscribers, and the blog grew into this book. Later the model in the book — «Management 3.0» — became an international movement of trainings and workshops.

One thing is important before you start: the book gives NO case studies, no lists of «correct practices» and no simple answers. The author calls his approach descriptive, not normative: his goal is that you understand how organisations and teams behave, so that you can invent your own solutions for your own situation.
keyPoints: Management 3.0 = complexity theory applied to agile teams
Descriptive approach: understanding first, your own recipes second
Written for managers and for developers who want to understand management
steps.example: Think about advice books like «do these five things and your team will be motivated». They fail in real life because your team, your product and your company are different. This book instead explains WHY motivation works the way it does — and then you design the five things yourself.

steps.title: Who it is for
steps.body:
The author defines his readers very precisely: managers who want to move their company to agile ways of working, and developers who already work in an agile way but want to understand management as a whole.

His starting point is uncomfortable for many companies. Research on agile adoption shows that the biggest obstacles are not technical: they are traditional change management, company culture, lack of support from leadership, poorly prepared people and external pressure. In other words — management. Teams find it very hard to work with Scrum, XP or Kanban when their leaders are stuck in old top-down habits.

The book is also unusual in its style. It is built on science — complexity theory, psychology, research — and it does not ask you to «open your heart» or repeat motivational mantras. It speaks to rational, analytical people, especially in technology companies. But the science comes with metaphors, drawings and jokes: managers are compared to gardeners, wizards and traffic officers, and the model itself is drawn as a six-eyed monster.

So you do not need to be a manager to benefit. If you are in a team, this gives you language to explain what is wrong and what could work better.
keyPoints: The main obstacles to Agile are management ones, not technical
Science-based, but written with metaphors and humour
Useful for team members too, not only for managers
steps.example: A team asks for permission to run their own retrospectives. The manager refuses: «I need to control the process». Nothing in Scrum can fix this — the blocker is a management belief, not a practice. This is exactly the situation the book is written for.

steps.title: Quiz: the approach
steps.body: Check that you understand the format.

quiz.question: Why does the book give no list of «standard practices to follow»?
options: The world is too complex for universal recipes: the goal is understanding, so you can build your own solutions for your context
The practices are a commercial secret
quiz.explanation: A descriptive approach instead of a normative one is a deliberate choice. It also matches complexity theory itself, which the whole book is built on.

steps.title: Why «Management 3.0»
steps.body:
The name is a joke about software versions: «Microsoft usually needs three releases before a product really works». The author believes that in its third version management finally has a solid scientific base.

Two insights of complexity science stand behind the name.

First: ALL ORGANISATIONS ARE NETWORKS. People can draw their company as a neat hierarchy of boxes, but in practice work happens through relationships — who talks to whom, who trusts whom, who asks whom for help. The org chart shows who signs documents; the network shows how things actually get done.

Second: MANAGEMENT IS MOSTLY ABOUT PEOPLE AND THEIR RELATIONSHIPS, not about department structures and profit reports. When you manage a complex social system, the connections matter more than the boxes.

From this follows the change of basic assumption: from hierarchies to networks. As the author writes, «the 21st century is the age of complexity», so organisations must be treated as living systems, not as machines. A machine you repair by replacing parts. A living system you influence by changing its conditions — light, water, food, space.

This also changes the meaning of «leadership». It stops being a fashionable title and becomes something simple: doing the right things and doing them right.
keyPoints: Organisations are networks, even when drawn as hierarchies
Management is about people and relationships first
Living system, not machine: change conditions, not parts
steps.example: A new employee needs an answer urgently. Formally they should ask their manager, who asks another manager, who asks a developer. In reality they write in a group chat and get the answer in five minutes from someone three departments away. That chat is the real organisation — the network.

steps.title: Princes: the false «leadership»
steps.body:
The subtitle of the book mentions «leadership» — a word the author says is used wrongly by two groups of people. The first group he calls, with irony, PRINCES.

Princes are top managers who claim that «leadership is something higher than management»: leaders inspire, managers only execute; leadership is «one level above». Appelo says this makes him uncomfortable every time a company calls its top managers «leaders».

His argument is simple. Every employee — from the president to the newest developer — can inspire colleagues and show a direction. Real leaders, by definition, have NO formal power over their followers: people follow them voluntarily. But no shareholder will hand money to a «leader» who has no formal authority at all. So the two things are different, and neither is «higher».

What actually happens: senior managers use «leadership» as a social myth that strengthens their position in the hierarchy. The author calls them princes because they believe their job title gives them more right to lead than everyone else — «and because they prefer shiny objects to common sense».

The practical lesson: do not confuse a title with influence. Influence is earned by clarity, competence and trust — and it is available to everyone.
keyPoints: A title does not create a leader; influence does
Real leaders have followers, not formal power over them
«Leadership» can be a myth that protects status
steps.example: In one company the CEO renamed all directors into «leaders» and nothing changed: the same orders, the same control. Meanwhile a senior developer with no title organised code reviews, mentoring and a shared style guide — and half the department followed her. Guess who was really leading.

steps.title: Priests: «we need no managers»
steps.body:
The second group are PRIESTS. They say the opposite of princes: management is unnecessary. They point at Wikipedia, Linux and other self-organised communities that achieved amazing results without managers, only with a shared goal and a vision.

The author's counter-argument is short and strong: none of these examples is a business. If nobody OWNS the assets of an organisation, then nobody needs to manage them. But shareholders will not be delighted if a self-organising biotech company decides to become a catering business.

From this he draws the key line: SELF-ORGANISATION IN ITSELF HAS NO VALUE. Self-organisation is a process — it can produce anything, good or bad. Somebody who cares about the result must judge whether what emerged is «good» or «bad» for the owners, the customers and the people. Managers exist because owners need someone to look after their business, and the opinion of employees about whether managers are needed is, in this sense, not the deciding factor.

And the belief «hierarchy is always bad, self-organisation is always good» is exactly that — a belief. The author calls these people priests because they preach faith, while the book shows there is no scientific basis for it.
keyPoints: Self-organisation has no value without a direction and someone responsible
Wikipedia and Linux are not businesses with owners of assets
«Hierarchy bad, self-organisation good» is faith, not science
steps.example: A team self-organises brilliantly and spends three months refactoring the codebase into a beautiful architecture — while the company loses its biggest client because a promised feature was never delivered. The self-organisation worked perfectly. The direction did not.

steps.title: Pragmatists: the position of the book
steps.body:
Between princes and priests the author puts a third group, and this is where he stands: PRAGMATISTS — «the common people».

The pragmatic position has three parts.

1. Every business needs management on behalf of the owners. Yes, managers should have leadership qualities — but management itself is a legitimate, necessary job, and there is nothing to be ashamed of in a hierarchy.

2. Many leadership roles are played by self-organising people WITHOUT manager titles, at every level of the company. These informal leaders must understand that the direction of self-organisation sometimes needs correction — and that this correction comes from owners through the authority given to managers.

3. Most of the real work happens inside a social network of equals: leaders and followers, not bosses and subordinates.

The formula worth remembering: COMMUNICATION GOES THROUGH NETWORKS, AUTHORITY GOES THROUGH THE HIERARCHY.

«I wrote this book for pragmatists», the author says. Not for those who worship hierarchy, and not for those who worship its absence.
keyPoints: Communication through networks, authority through hierarchy
Hierarchy is a necessity, not a virtue and not a sin
Informal leaders are real, but direction still needs an owner
steps.example: A team decides on its own how to build a feature (network, self-organisation). The decision to invest six months into a new product line is made by managers who answer to the owners (hierarchy, authority). Both mechanisms work at the same time, on different questions.

steps.title: Quiz: princes, priests, pragmatists
steps.body: Sort the positions.

quiz.question: «Our team needs no managers at all — look at Wikipedia!» Who says this, and what is weak in this position?
options: A prince; the weakness is arrogance
A priest; the weakness: those self-organised examples are not businesses with owners, and self-organisation without someone responsible for results has no value
A pragmatist; this is the correct view
Nobody; it is a quote from the manifesto
quiz.explanation: A classic priest position. The pragmatic answer: yes, self-organisation is powerful, but someone must be responsible to the owners for direction and results.

steps.title: Apply it to your own experience
steps.body:
Think about organisations where you worked or studied, and answer (out loud or in writing):

1. Where did the REAL communication happen — through the official hierarchy, or through a network of friends and group chats?
2. Did you meet any «princes» (title = right to lead) or «priests» (management = evil)?
3. Who was an informal leader without a title — and how did that look?

This exercise makes the main idea concrete: hierarchy on paper, network in reality.

steps.title: Map of the whole book
steps.body:
It helps to see the whole map, even if your edition contains only the first chapters.

• Chapter 1 — the introduction: why linear thinking gives wrong answers in complex systems, and the first presentation of the Management 3.0 model.
• Chapters 2–3 — the two foundations: a review of agile software development, and complexity theory itself.
• Chapters 4–15 — the six components of the model, two chapters each. In every pair the first chapter is more theoretical and the second more practical: energise people (4–5), empower teams (6–7), align constraints (8–9), develop competence (10–11), grow structure (12–13), improve everything (14–15).
• Chapter 16 — the summary and a comparison with other management models, under the title «All models are wrong, but some are useful».

The author says the chapters do not depend heavily on each other, so in theory you can read them in any order — but in practice it is easiest to go from the beginning. He also points out that the practical chapters together are longer than the theoretical ones, and that every chapter ends with a section called «Reflect and act» with concrete tasks. We use those tasks in this roadmap.

One more useful detail: the book has a companion site, management30.com, with extra materials and the original illustrations.
keyPoints: Two foundations, six components (theory + practice), one conclusion
Every chapter ends with practical «Reflect and act» tasks
You can navigate by problem, not only read linearly
steps.example: If you only have 30 minutes and a very concrete problem — say, low motivation in the team — you can jump straight to chapters 4–5 («energise people») and still get value. The map tells you where to jump.

steps.title: Module summary
steps.body: Fix the start in your memory.

quiz.question: Which sentence describes the spirit of the book best?
options: «Do these 10 practices and your team will be Agile»
«Understand how people and complex systems behave, and build your own management recipes — there are no universal solutions»
quiz.explanation: Descriptive approach + complexity science + a pragmatic view of hierarchy and networks — that is the foundation of Management 3.0.

title: Management 1.0 → 2.0 → 3.0
intro: Three versions of management: hierarchies, fashionable add-ons, and complex systems. See why «upgrades» could not fix the old architecture.

steps.title: Management 1.0 = hierarchies
steps.body:
The first version of management has many names: «scientific management», «command and control», Taylorism. The idea behind all of them is the same: the organisation is designed and steered FROM THE TOP DOWN, and real power belongs to a small group of people at the top.

The author's picture of it is deliberately unkind. At the top of the hierarchy you find the highest salaries, the biggest egos and the most expensive office chairs. At the bottom there is much less money, much less responsibility — and, as a result, very little motivation to do good work. People at the bottom are treated as executors of decisions made somewhere above them.

Then he adds an important historical point. To compensate for the «risk» of top positions, senior managers received the power to influence their own bonuses. In many cases this improved their personal wealth far more than the results of their companies — and broken bonus systems became one of the contributing factors to the global financial crisis.

His conclusion: Management 1.0 is still the most widespread version in the world, but it has serious defects. It is outdated and needs an update — not because it is old-fashioned, but because it produces bad results with modern, creative, complex work.
keyPoints: 1.0 = design and control from the top, power in few hands
Bottom of the hierarchy: less money, less responsibility, less motivation
Still the most common version — and the least suited to creative work
steps.example: A classic 1.0 sign: a manager who says «I need every task estimated in hours and reported daily» for a team doing research work nobody has done before. The reports feel like control, but they measure guesses, not progress.

steps.title: Management 2.0 = following fashions
steps.body:
Eventually people noticed that 1.0 works badly outside of very standard situations. So a whole generation of models and extensions appeared: balanced scorecards, Six Sigma, the theory of constraints, total quality management and many more.

The author's diagnosis is precise: these are ADD-ONS on top of 1.0. They still assume that organisations are steered from the top and that their purpose is to help senior managers improve the «design» of the company. Sometimes they work, sometimes they do not.

In parallel came the other branch of 2.0: books about the art and craft of management — «The One Minute Manager», «21 Irrefutable Laws of Leadership», «Good to Great». They contain basic principles that managers are supposed to follow, plus advice to practise more and gain experience. Again: sometimes helpful, sometimes not. As the author jokes, «sets of recommendations change more often than nappies on a baby».

The conclusion of the section: Management 2.0 is the same familiar 1.0 with a number of add-ons that soften the pain caused by the old system. But the architecture underneath is still the outdated hierarchy — and the fundamental assumptions were never questioned.
keyPoints: 2.0 = 1.0 plus fashionable add-ons and advice books
The assumptions (top-down steering) were never questioned
Tools change fast; architecture stays — that is why results stay too
steps.example: A company introduces OKRs, engagement surveys and a leadership academy. Two years later people still wait for the boss to decide everything, and OKRs are set top-down in the same old way. The tools changed; the operating system did not.

steps.title: Quiz: why 2.0 failed
steps.body: A key diagnosis.

quiz.question: A company uses Six Sigma, a KPI system and reads leadership bestsellers — but teams still wait for orders from above. Which «version» is this, and why?
options: 2.0: add-ons on top of an unchanged top-down architecture, so nothing fundamental has changed
quiz.explanation: The test is not the name of the tools, but the basic assumption: who makes decisions and where information flows. While everything comes from the top, it is 1.0 or 2.0, no matter how many sigmas there are.

steps.title: Management 3.0 = complex systems
steps.body:
Over the last decades a new field grew: COMPLEXITY THEORY. It started in mathematics and biology, then moved into economics and sociology. The author calls this a major breakthrough and quotes the physicist Stephen Hawking, who said that the 21st century will be «the century of complexity».

What does this give to management? Three things.

First, a SCIENTIFIC approach to studying complex systems — including software projects and organisations as a whole. Not opinions of successful CEOs, but research into how systems with many interacting parts actually behave.

Second, a new picture of the organisation: a network of living interactions. Companies are drawn as hierarchies, but they behave as networks. Complexity theory applied to social systems says management must deal first of all with people and their relationships, not with department structures and profit lines.

Third, a clearer meaning of the word «leadership»: managers doing the right things and doing them right — and thinking in terms of systems rather than machines.

The author is honest about what stays: the earlier add-ons of 2.0 are still useful. What must change is the base hypothesis — from hierarchies to networks. Hence «3.0»: not new decoration, but a new foundation.
keyPoints: 3.0 stands on complexity science, not on opinions
Base hypothesis changes from hierarchy to network
Old tools remain useful; the foundation is what is new
steps.example: A manager wants fewer bugs. In 1.0 they would introduce a rule and punish violations. In 3.0 they ask: what in our system produces bugs — pressure, unclear requirements, no time for review? — and change those conditions. Same goal, completely different lever.

steps.title: Quiz: three versions
steps.body: Put them in order.

quiz.question: Match: (a) «the boss knows best, just do it»; (b) «the boss knows best, but now he has a KPI dashboard»; (c) «the team is a living network; management works with people and relationships».
quiz.explanation: 1.0 is pure hierarchy; 2.0 is the same hierarchy with add-ons; 3.0 changes the basic assumption to a network view.

steps.title: Practice: diagnose an organisation you know
steps.body:
Take an organisation you know well (work, university, a club, volunteering) and write a short diagnosis:

1. How are decisions made: top-down? by KPI? by teams?
2. Are there «2.0 add-ons» (metrics, frameworks, rules) that did not change anything real?
3. Where can you see the «network» — the real paths that information and work follow?
4. Verdict: 1.0 / 2.0 / 3.0 (or a mix — which parts?).

Bonus question: what ONE change could move this organisation half a step towards 3.0?
keyPoints: Diagnose by decisions and information flow, not by slogans

steps.title: Why this matters for you
steps.body:
The model is not only for CEOs. It is practical at any level, and in three different roles.

As a TEAM MEMBER: you get language for what you already feel. When a manager micro-manages a creative task, you can explain why it lowers the result instead of raising it — and propose an alternative (clear goal + autonomy + short feedback loop) instead of just being frustrated.

As a LEADER — now or later: you get a job description that fits complex work. Not «assign tasks and check them», but: give people energy, give teams authority, set clear constraints, grow competence, build the structure where information flows, and improve the system continuously.

As a THINKING PERSON: you see the same principles outside work. A family, a student group, a volunteer project — all are complex social systems where detailed top-down planning fails, where small experiments beat big plans, and where relationships matter more than boxes.

The author says it directly: it does not matter whether you are a project manager, a team leader, a CTO or a programmer. We are all trying to manage the environment around us — «let us learn to do it well».
keyPoints: Works at any level: member, leader, or outside work
Gives you both language and a practical job description
Small changes in conditions beat big changes in structure
steps.example: You cannot change your company's structure. But you can start one thing: ask your team what would make their work smoother, pick one answer and try it for two weeks. That is Management 3.0 at the smallest possible scale — and it is real.

steps.title: Module summary
steps.body: The main point of the three versions.

quiz.question: What is the REAL difference of Management 3.0 from 1.0 and 2.0 (not a cosmetic one)?
options: A different basic assumption: the organisation is a complex living network, so you manage conditions and people instead of details from above; 1.0 and 2.0 stand on hierarchy
There is no hierarchy at all
quiz.explanation: Hierarchy does not disappear in 3.0 (authority still goes through it), but it stops being the model of how the organisation really works. This is a change of foundation, not of decoration.

title: Chapter 1a · Determinism and complexity
intro: Why «everything goes to plan» is an illusion: determinism, its successes and its limits, and the tricky sister of predictability called complexity.

steps.title: The story of a millionaire on paper
steps.body:
Chapter 1 opens with a confession. During the dotcom years the author's internet startup was valued by private investors at 10 million euros, and he owned 70% of that «financial fiction». He was even given the title «entrepreneur of the year», because he presented his vision so convincingly. The colourful graphs of expected income and costs looked fantastic — on paper.

Then reality arrived. The invested money did not turn into profit. New content did not bring more visitors. Hiring more programmers did not speed up development in any noticeable way. Partnership agreements with other sites did not increase revenue — income actually fell BELOW the level before the investment round. All attempts to promote the site failed. And when the dotcom bubble burst, that was the end.

The epigraph of the chapter is from H.L. Mencken: «For every complex problem there is an answer that is clear, simple and wrong.»

This story sets up the main theme of the whole book: however carefully you plan, reality will almost certainly develop differently. The system you operate in does not care about your plans. You may believe you can go from point A to point B — and in theory you may be right. But theories rarely work in practice, because predictability has a treacherous sister called complexity.
keyPoints: A detailed plan does not create a predictable result
The system does not care about your plans
Predictability has a sister: complexity
steps.example: Think of any project where the plan said «three months» and reality said «eight». Usually nobody was lazy or incompetent. The plan simply assumed a predictable world, and the world was complex.

steps.title: Determinism: where our faith in plans comes from
steps.body:
Our belief that things normally go according to plan comes from an inborn preference for DETERMINISM. Determinism says: «future events inevitably follow from previous ones according to the laws of nature». The cause of any event is another event that happened earlier. Logically this means: if we know everything about the current state and all transition rules, we can calculate the future.

And determinism has been extraordinarily successful. Using Newton's mechanics, scientists confidently predict the return of Halley's Comet to the solar system in 2061. The method was so powerful that Immanuel Kant declared universal determinism a necessary condition of any scientific knowledge.

It works in software too. Developers design and predict the behaviour of their programs; they change code to change behaviour after compilation and deployment. If we ignore bugs, operating system crashes, power failures and unskilled users, their predictions are often quite accurate. The same determinism let the author correctly predict that his own project would go bankrupt without new customers.

But here is the puzzle. We can predict a comet decades ahead — and we cannot predict the weather one month ahead. We cannot predict the result of a complex combination of desired features, available time and required resources. And we could not predict when new customers would appear.
keyPoints: Determinism: know the state and the rules, calculate the future
It works brilliantly — for some kinds of systems
Comet: yes. Weather next month: no. That gap is the whole point
steps.example: Compare two questions: «how much disk space will this file take?» (deterministic — calculate it) and «will users like this feature?» (complex — you can only try). Managers get in trouble when they treat the second like the first.

steps.title: Complexity is not about big numbers
steps.body:
The answer to the puzzle is COMPLEXITY. The author uses a family metaphor: if predictability is the polite, obedient neighbour's son, then complexity is his wilful, unpredictable younger sister. Predictability lets you go to work, plan meetings, do sport and watch television. Complexity turns your interaction with the world into unexpected chaos full of surprises.

A very common confusion: people mix up complexity with the problem of LARGE NUMBERS (many events happening at once). Complex phenomena do not require many elements. Take a water molecule: two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom. Nothing complicated. And yet such a simple structure produces surprising complex phenomena — fluidity, density effects and other physical and chemical behaviours that cannot be easily explained from the behaviour of individual atoms. Three water molecules are already enough for the system to show complex behaviour; the famous three-body problem in physics is another example.

Since the 17th century science advanced under the flag of determinism. Complexity as a subject appeared in the 20th century: dynamic systems theory, chaos theory, network theory, game theory and others explained WHY some phenomena cannot be predicted and why some events cannot be planned or calculated in advance — they can only be tried or observed. Together this field is called complexity theory.
keyPoints: Complexity ≠ many elements: three can be enough
Some things cannot be calculated — only tried or observed
Complexity theory = the science of exactly those systems
steps.example: Three people in a group chat are enough for complexity: A jokes, B takes it seriously, C defends B, and by evening you have a conflict nobody planned. Three elements, unpredictable outcome.

steps.title: Quiz: calculate or try
steps.body: The key distinction of the chapter.

quiz.question: Which of these belongs to the world of COMPLEXITY (you cannot calculate it exactly in advance — you can only try and observe)?
options: The path of a thrown ball
How a team will react to a new bonus system
How much memory an array of a million numbers needs
quiz.explanation: Ball, comet and array are deterministic. The reaction of living people in a network of relationships is a complex system: you can only make rough predictions and test them by experiment.

steps.title: Good news for managers
steps.body:
The development of complexity theory is genuinely good news for team leaders, project managers and everyone else who leads work in companies that build software. It means a SCIENTIFIC approach now exists for studying complex systems, including software development and the management of organisations.

What this changes in daily practice:

• Your projects do not follow the plan not because you are a bad manager, but because they are complex systems — and all complex systems behave like that. This removes a lot of unnecessary guilt and blame.

• Instead of being ashamed of deviations, you can build a process that LIVES with unpredictability: short cycles, small experiments, careful observation, quick adaptation. This is exactly what agile methods do.

• This is not «chaos instead of order». It is a different kind of order. A gardener does not assemble a plant from parts; she creates the conditions in which it grows — soil, light, water, space — and then observes and adjusts.

The author agrees with Hawking that complexity is the key paradigm of the 21st century, and adds bitterly that for him personally this insight came exactly 10 million euros too late.
keyPoints: Unpredictability is a property of the system, not your failure
Answer: short cycles, experiments, observation, adaptation
Gardener, not mechanic: create conditions, then adjust
steps.example: Instead of planning a year of features in detail, a team plans two weeks in detail, three months roughly and a year as direction. When reality changes — and it does — only two weeks of planning are wasted, not a year.

steps.title: Practice: calculation vs experiment
steps.body:
Take a project you are working on now (at work, at university, or personal) and split its parts into two columns:

1. CAN BE CALCULATED: what is deterministic here? (budget with known prices, duration of known operations, technical limits)

2. CAN ONLY BE TRIED: what is complex? (how people react, demand, whether an idea «works», how long new-for-you work really takes)

Look at column 2. How many of these things have you been trying to «calculate» with detailed planning? Choose one and design a small EXPERIMENT instead of a plan: what is the cheapest way to test reality?
keyPoints: Two columns: calculation / experiment
For complex things: a small test instead of a big plan

steps.title: Module summary
steps.body: Put the chapter together.

quiz.question: Why did the author's 30-page business plan turn out to be «carefully checked nonsense»?
options: The plan used deterministic calculation for a complex system (market, people, bubble) — such systems cannot be calculated in advance
He was unlucky with his team
quiz.explanation: The author believed in his plan («I made it — how could it be wrong?»). The problem was not the quality of the calculation, but using calculation for something complex.

title: Chapter 1b · Our linear thinking
intro: Why the brain sees simple causes where there are none: the causality fallacy, the wish to control, and the heritage of «scientific management».

steps.title: The brain is a cause-finding machine
steps.body:
Applying complexity theory to real problems runs into an obstacle inside our own heads: the brain PREFERS simple cause-and-effect links and ignores complexity.

The author refers to research («Born believers: How your brain creates God») showing that the human brain is excessively oriented towards establishing causal links — so much that we see them where they do not exist. Children think sharp rocks exist so that animals can scratch themselves, and rivers exist so that people can travel by boat. Our brain seems built to find purpose and causality everywhere, even with no grounds at all.

The evolutionary explanation is quoted directly in the book: «You hear a rustle in the bushes and conclude that someone is hiding there.» An excessive tendency to see causes and effects gives an advantage for survival. If the area is full of predators, detecting them in nine cases out of ten is not enough. It is better to over-insure and run away, even if sometimes the danger is imaginary. The price of that over-insurance is low.

So the habit of seeing causes everywhere is not a defect — it is an old survival advantage. The problem is that in a complex modern world it constantly leads us to confident, simple and wrong conclusions.
keyPoints: The brain finds causes even where there are none
This was a survival advantage, not stupidity
In complex environments it produces confident wrong answers
steps.example: Sales dropped after a new manager joined. The brain instantly produces: «the new manager caused it». Season, competitors, a price change and a broken checkout page do not even get considered — the first story felt complete.

steps.title: The causality fallacy
steps.body:
Our brain is hard-wired to prefer LINEAR thinking — the idea that effects are predictable if causes are known — over NON-LINEAR thinking, the hypothesis that reality is much more complicated. At school we are taught to solve linear equations; the non-linear ones, which are far more common in practice, are ignored simply because they are much harder.

It is easier for us to accept «he did it» than «some things just happen». If there is problem B, we assume that event A caused it. Bankers caused the financial crisis. Immigrants caused unemployment. The manager caused the bad atmosphere in the company. CO2 emissions caused the melting of polar ice. The project team missed the deadline because somebody worked badly.

Linear thinking perceives the world as a space filled with easily explainable events with simple causes and simple effects. Gerald Weinberg calls this the CAUSALITY FALLACY.

The practical detector is simple: whenever a complex question («why is the project late?», «why did quality drop?») has ONE convenient answer with ONE guilty party, you are probably looking at this fallacy. Real complex systems almost always have multiple interacting causes — and often the cause and the effect reinforce each other in a loop.
keyPoints: One problem = one guilty person is a red flag
Non-linear reality is more common than linear
Look for loops: causes and effects often feed each other
steps.example: «We are late because QA is slow.» Look closer: requirements arrive late, so development finishes late, so QA gets everything at once, so QA is slow, so developers stop trusting deadlines, so estimates get padded. A loop, not a culprit.

steps.title: Quiz: catch the fallacy
steps.body: Diagnose linear thinking.

quiz.question: «Sales dropped because the marketing manager ran a bad campaign.» What is this, from the chapter's point of view?
options: Probably the causality fallacy: in a complex system (market, season, competitors, product, prices) one convenient cause and one guilty person were selected
Correct, if the campaign really was bad
quiz.explanation: Maybe the campaign was weak — but «it caused the drop in sales» requires excluding a dozen other factors. The brain loves a ready-made culprit.

steps.title: The wish to control and scientific management
steps.body:
Our mental dependence on determinism pushes people to look for ways of CONTROL — ways to guarantee that desirable events happen and undesirable ones do not. The logic feels obvious: if situation A produces event B, and situation A′ produces event C which is better than B, then we simply need to turn A into A′.

Engineers and other technically-minded people are especially receptive to ideas based on controllability. It was engineers who created SCIENTIFIC MANAGEMENT — management by giving orders and controlling their execution — which dominated from the beginning of the 20th century. And it was engineers who invented the control systems that still exist in many organisations today.

But here is the crucial limit, stated plainly in the book: control systems are effective ONLY for repeated operations that do not require much thinking. They do NOT work in situations that need a creative approach, such as developing new products.

The author adds a sharp joke: it would be only fair if engineers now pulled us out of the management swamp into which they once dragged us.

For you this means: before applying any control mechanism, ask what kind of work it will touch. Repetitive and known? Control helps. Creative and uncertain? Control destroys.
keyPoints: Control is effective for repeatable work without thinking
It fails for creative work — like product development
Ask first: what kind of work am I trying to control?
steps.example: A checklist before surgery or before deploying to production — excellent use of control. A daily report of hours spent per subtask in a research project — control applied to creativity, which mostly produces well-formatted fiction.

steps.title: Quiz: where control fits
steps.body: A fine line.

quiz.question: Where are classic control systems (detailed instructions, norms, checking execution) APPROPRIATE?
options: In repeated standard operations (assembly line, accounting routine, safety checklist)
quiz.explanation: The author does not say «control is evil»: for repeated work it is effective. The mistake is using it for creative work with complex dynamics, like product development.

steps.title: The illusion of design from above
steps.body:
Determinism in management pushes managers to «design» the result: first define the outcome in detail, then plan everything from the top down, then make the parts of the organisation interact so that the plan comes true. And the bigger the organisation, the more effort is spent on analysing the behaviour of its parts to force them into the planned interaction.

The author does not exclude himself. He writes that he happily built a world of illusions based on advance design and top-down planning. His business plan — which even won professional awards — consisted of 30 pages of «carefully checked nonsense» describing in detail how they would get rich. And he adds the sentence that every planner should remember: «At that moment we believed in this business plan. After all, since I developed it, how could it be wrong?»

The pattern is everywhere today: annual roadmaps planned week by week, detailed specifications written a year ahead, «master plans of transformation» designed by consultants.

This does not make planning useless. But a very detailed plan applied to a complex system gives you a FEELING of control, not control itself — and the feeling is expensive, because it hides the need to observe reality and adapt.
keyPoints: Detailed top-down design = the feeling of control, not control
«I made the plan, so how could it be wrong?» — a warning sign
Planning stays useful; pretending to know the future does not
steps.example: Two teams plan a year. Team A writes 40 pages of detail. Team B writes one page of direction plus a two-week plan and a monthly review. After six months Team A is defending its plan; Team B has changed course twice and is closer to the goal.

steps.title: Practice: «Reflect and act» from chapter 1
steps.body:
The author ends the chapter with practical tasks. Here they are, slightly adapted:

1. Take a real UNSOLVED problem from your professional life. Write down what you think its cause is. Now be honest: are you sure this is the ONLY cause? Why? Would all the people involved agree with your explanation? Do the same analysis for two or three of your most important problems — check that you are not oversimplifying and not «fixing» a wrongly identified cause.

2. If your team uses root-cause methods (for example «five whys»), discuss with colleagues the tendency of these methods to oversimplify. In complex systems causes are MULTIPLE, and cause and effect are often in a circular relationship. Then no cause is «the main one». Organise this discussion.
keyPoints: Test every «cause»: only one? would everyone agree? am I simplifying?
«Five whys» in complex systems has real limits

steps.title: Module summary
steps.body: The main point about linearity.

quiz.question: Why does root-cause analysis have a built-in weakness in complex systems?
options: In complex systems causes are multiple, and cause and effect can be circular — so «the main cause» often does not exist
quiz.explanation: It is still a useful tool — but it looks only backwards and tends to simplify. Knowing these limits is non-linear thinking in action.

title: Chapter 1c · Reductionism and holism
intro: Two ways to understand a system: take it apart, or look at the whole. Why both are needed — and why neither is enough.

steps.title: Reductionism: take it apart
keyPoints: Reductionism = understand the whole through its parts
It built modern technology — and has a real limit
Consciousness, economy, climate, software projects: all resist it
steps.example: You can know every function in a codebase and still not predict what the product will feel like to a user. The behaviour lives in the interactions — between modules, between people, between the product and the world.

steps.title: The mechanical duck
steps.body:
The book illustrates this with a famous old drawing: a mechanical duck taken apart into springs, gears and tubes. The caption is «an example of reductionism that went too far».

The point is easy to feel. However carefully you look at the deconstructed duck, you will have serious difficulty identifying inside it the levers, bearings and gears responsible for walking, swimming and quacking. And yet, when you see the object in a park, you instantly know: this is a duck.

This has far-reaching consequences for managers of complex systems. Knowing everything about the components does not give you the behaviour of the whole. The team is not the sum of the CVs. The product is not the sum of the features. The company is not the sum of the departments.

So when someone proposes to fix a complex problem by «optimising each part», the duck should come to mind. Optimising every component separately very often makes the whole system worse — a phenomenon so common that Lean thinkers gave it a name: local optimisation.
keyPoints: Knowing the parts ≠ knowing the system
Optimising each part often damages the whole
When someone says «optimise every component» — remember the duck
steps.example: Every department hits its own KPI: sales sells more, support closes tickets faster, development ships more features. And the customer is unhappy, because nobody owns the end-to-end experience. All parts optimised, whole degraded.

steps.title: Quiz: the limit of reductionism
steps.body: Where does the method stop?

quiz.question: You know exactly what every developer in your team does, hour by hour. Does this mean you can predict the result of the project?
options: Yes, that is exactly how prediction works
No: a complex system is not the sum of its parts — the interactions create behaviour you cannot see in the components
Yes, if you also know their salaries
quiz.explanation: This is the classic mistake: perfect knowledge of components does not give you the behaviour of the whole. It is exactly the duck problem.

steps.title: Greedy reductionism and hierarchical reductionism
steps.body:
Even convinced reductionists eventually gave up the idea that everything reduces to the behaviour of components.

The philosopher Daniel Dennett introduced the term GREEDY REDUCTIONISM for the extreme version: attempts to derive the behaviour of a system fully from the interactions between its parts. His example of the style: «hyperlinks are nothing more than electrons, and electrons do not really exist». The author adds his own joke: if greedy reductionists are right, then they do not exist either, which removes all their ridiculous arguments.

The evolutionary biologist Richard Dawkins proposed a compromise: HIERARCHICAL REDUCTIONISM. A complex system can be represented as a hierarchy of levels, where events at each level can be explained by the behaviour of components ONE LEVEL BELOW — and only one. Following this logic, you cannot explain the failure of your project by quarks and leptons.

This is a very practical rule for a manager. To understand a team, look at people and their relationships — one level down. To understand an organisation, look at teams and their interactions. Do not jump levels: neither downwards into neurons, nor upwards into «the market is difficult».
keyPoints: Greedy reductionism explains everything by the smallest parts — and fails
Hierarchical reductionism: explain a level by the level just below
Practical rule: to understand a team, look at people and relationships
steps.example: A team misses deadlines. Useful: look at the level below — people, dependencies, interruptions, unclear tasks. Useless: «people are like that these days» (too high) or «it's because of how the brain processes stress» (too low).

steps.title: Holism: the idea of wholeness
steps.body:
HOLISM as a theory says the opposite of reductionism: the behaviour of a system cannot be reduced to the sum of the behaviours of its separate parts. It is decisively determined by the properties of the system as a single whole.

People usually treat holism as the enemy of reductionism. But scientists who study complex systems say something more interesting: complexity is the LINK between the two approaches, and each of them is necessary but not sufficient.

The chapter adds a distinction worth remembering. Even if you can find the cause of a problem (reductionism), you cannot always design a system where the problem is impossible (constructionism). You can establish the cause of a specific case of heart failure — but you will never build a heart that is principally immune to heart failure.

And there is an honest note about root-cause analysis, in a grey box in the book: is it useless? No — it is extremely useful. Its limitation is that it is turned exclusively towards the PAST. It helps solve problems that already happened and prevent their repetition. It does not help predict what exactly may go wrong in the future.
keyPoints: Complexity is the bridge: both approaches needed, neither sufficient
Finding a cause ≠ being able to design the problem away
Root-cause analysis looks backwards; it does not predict
steps.example: A post-mortem after an outage is valuable: you find the cause and remove it. But no number of post-mortems will tell you what the next outage will be — for that you need resilience, not analysis: monitoring, redundancy, small releases.

steps.title: Quiz: holism vs reductionism
steps.body: Check the balance.

quiz.question: Which statement matches the book's position?
options: Reductionism is wrong, only the holistic view works
Holism is mysticism, only analysis of parts works
Both approaches are necessary and neither is enough on its own; complexity connects them
quiz.explanation: The book is not against analysis. It is against ONLY analysis. You need both: study the parts and look at the whole.

steps.title: Hierarchical management and levels
steps.body:
Holism and hierarchical reductionism agree on one thing: not everything in the behaviour of a complex system can be explained by events at lower levels. Every level has its own properties that are not reducible to the levels below.

For managers this has serious consequences. Someone who knows everything about ONE level of a hierarchical system may be insufficiently qualified to work at other levels of the same system, because different knowledge is required.

The book's examples are memorable. A molecular biologist may be an unqualified gardener: knowing how living organisms work at the level of cells, genes and RNA does not imply the ability to take care of a garden. And a good gardener does not need to know anything about chromosomes and the genome. In exactly the same way, a CEO may have extensive knowledge of running a company and be completely helpless in coaching and other people-management skills.

The conclusion: managing an organisation requires completely different knowledge and experience than managing people — although SOME understanding of how the system works at lower levels can be useful.
keyPoints: Each level has its own properties and requires its own knowledge
Expert at one level is not automatically competent at another
Managing an organisation ≠ managing people; both are real skills
steps.example: A brilliant engineer is promoted to manager and fails. Nothing is wrong with the person: the new level needs different knowledge. Promotion without new skills is the classic mistake this idea explains.

steps.title: The law of leaky abstractions
steps.body:
The software engineer Joel Spolsky offered the LAW OF LEAKY ABSTRACTIONS as an explanation of why components at higher levels can behave unexpectedly because of events at lower levels — even though the higher levels should, in theory, be isolated from them.

A typical sign in programming is an incomprehensible error message. The book shows a small drawing of an error window that says: «ERROR: no error».

The author extends the idea with humour to himself: his own consciousness regularly becomes a victim of temporary confusion, déjà vu, forgetfulness and randomly surfacing memories — failures in low-level neural circuits that leak into the higher level he calls «my thinking». He does not need to analyse neurons to think satisfactorily, but the leaks happen anyway.

And the management version: to run a company, a CEO does not necessarily have to be effective at communicating with people, PROVIDED that communication is delegated to a reliable team of managers (this is where CEOs differ from product managers, project managers and team leaders, who must talk to colleagues every day). But in case low-level problems do break through to a higher level — in other words, when a leaky abstraction occurs — some communication skills can be very useful.
keyPoints: Higher levels are never fully isolated from lower ones
Delegation is fine — leaks still reach you
That is why leaders keep needing people and communication skills
steps.example: An unclear message in a group chat (low level) leads two teams to build the same thing (mid level), which delays a release promised to a client (high level). No architecture diagram shows this path — but it is exactly how the leak travels.

steps.title: Practice: find a leaky abstraction
keyPoints: Every abstraction leaks somewhere — find yours

steps.title: Module summary
steps.body: Fix the main ideas.

quiz.question: Which combination is the correct conclusion of this chapter?
options: Analyse only the parts — the whole will follow
Look only at the whole — details are noise
Use both: analyse parts (one level down) and look at the system as a whole; expect abstractions to leak
Complex systems cannot be studied at all
quiz.explanation: One level down for analysis, the whole for behaviour, and constant respect for leaks between levels — a practical summary of chapter 1.

title: Chapter 1d · Agile management and the model
intro: What happens when hierarchical management meets complex systems — and the six views of the Management 3.0 model.

steps.title: Agile management is born
steps.body:
When hierarchical management meets complex systems and non-linear thinking, we arrive in the area the author calls AGILE MANAGEMENT. It is the logical complement to agile methods of software development, which were created in the 1990s by several groups and individuals.

Why were they needed? Because the deterministic approach — based on careful control, detailed up-front design and top-down planning — kept producing failures. Despite very intensive management, the result in many cases was software that worked extremely badly.

Agile methods have roots in complexity theory: they recognise that causal determinism is not sufficient for successful projects. Well-known agile concepts like SELF-ORGANISATION and EMERGENCE are taken directly from the literature on complex systems. People who practise agile methods understand that a constructionist approach guarantees failure. Only continuous identification of problems that appear during a project, and the removal of their causes, allows the project to develop step by step and finally produce a successful product.

The author's comparison is warm and accurate: «It is like the process of growing up, or of raising children.» You cannot design a child in advance; you can create conditions, observe, respond and keep adjusting.
keyPoints: Agile management = hierarchy meets complexity and non-linear thinking
Self-organisation and emergence come from complexity science
Growing, not constructing: create conditions, observe, adapt
steps.example: Nobody plans a child's personality in a specification. You create conditions, watch what emerges, and adapt constantly. Complex products grow the same way — which is why fixed two-year plans keep failing.

steps.title: The manager as the obstacle
steps.body:
Agile projects show excellent results in terms of return on investment. And yet, many managers around the world block agile project management and agile methods inside their companies.

Research and surveys quoted in the book show that the main obstacles on the path of adopting agile software development are: traditional change-management methods, organisational culture, lack of support from leadership, low preparedness of personnel, and external pressure. Managers are responsible for most of these things.

The author states the consequence without softening it: if you trust the available reports — and he has no reason to doubt them — then managers all over the world are more of a problem than a part of the solution. And, sadly, this is not specific to agile software development: the same happens with any serious organisational change.

His position in this book is therefore explicit: when such changes are needed, traditional management is the problem, not the solution. The same point was made many years earlier by W. Edwards Deming. That is exactly why a theory of agile management is needed — a theory that fits well with agile methods of building software.
keyPoints: Main adoption blockers are managerial: culture, support, preparation
Traditional management becomes the problem during change
This is why agile methods need a matching management theory
steps.example: A team adopts Scrum, but the manager still assigns tasks personally, changes priorities mid-sprint and asks for hour-level estimates. The framework is in place, the operating system is not. Within a year the company concludes «Scrum doesn't work here».

steps.title: Quiz: the real blocker
steps.body: Check the diagnosis.

quiz.question: A company tries Scrum for a year, but nothing improves. According to the book, where should you look FIRST?
options: At management: culture, top-down control, lack of leadership support and preparation
At the size of the backlog
quiz.explanation: Research quoted in the book puts management culture and support at the top of the list of obstacles. Practices alone do not survive in a 1.0 environment.

steps.title: No «theory of everything»
steps.body:
Is there a theory that can help managers work in an agile environment? Many management «theories» proposed in recent decades are not theories in the strict scientific sense. A real scientific theory must not only point at the existence of some natural phenomena, but also make testable statements about the observable world, predicting what events should be expected BEFORE they can be observed. Most management theories do not meet this expectation — they are sets of techniques and advice rather than descriptions of how the world works. In this sense the theory of constraints is a good example: not a scientific theory but a management philosophy that offers ways to optimise processes.

The author admits that he once hoped to invent a «theory of everything» about software development management — a single complete model of how all teams work. Looking back, he says his thinking at that time was a victim of a leaky abstraction.

He abandoned the goal for two reasons. First, many theories about how people work in teams already exist; this field is known as SOCIAL COMPLEXITY. Second, complexity theory itself says that any attempt to create a single theory describing complex systems is doomed to fail.

His reaction is a small lesson in itself: «It is impossible to do. Great! So I can start working on something else.»
keyPoints: A single complete theory of complex systems is impossible
Most management «theories» are technique sets, not theories
Keeping several partial models beats hunting for the perfect one
steps.example: Compare two managers. One searches for the one framework that will finally fix everything, adopting a new one every year. The other keeps several partial models and picks the one that fits the situation. The second one is doing science; the first is doing hope.

steps.title: The Management 3.0 model: six views
steps.body:
The model is drawn in the book as a friendly six-eyed monster (figure 1.4). Each «eye» is one view on teams and organisations. Every component gets two chapters — one theoretical and one practical.

1. ENERGISE PEOPLE. People are the most important part of an organisation, and managers must do everything in their power so that employees stay active, creative and motivated.

2. EMPOWER TEAMS. Teams can self-organise, and this requires empowerment, authorisation and trust from management.

3. ALIGN CONSTRAINTS. Self-organisation can produce anything at all — including something useless — so it is necessary to give people a clear purpose and defined goals, and to protect them and the shared resources.

4. DEVELOP COMPETENCE. Teams cannot achieve their goals if team members are not capable enough, so managers must contribute to the development of competence and discipline.

5. GROW STRUCTURE. Many teams operate inside the context of a complex organisation, so it is important to build a structure that supports communication — the right social-network structure.

6. IMPROVE EVERYTHING. People, teams and organisations need to improve continuously, in order to delay failure as long as possible.

Six words to remember: energise, empower, align, develop, grow, improve.
keyPoints: Six views = a practical job description for a manager
Each has a theory chapter and a practice chapter
Diagnose by symptom: each symptom points to one view
steps.example: Use it as a diagnostic checklist. Team demotivated → view 1. Team waits for permission → view 2. Team busy but building the wrong thing → view 3. Team wants but cannot → view 4. Teams collide → view 5. Same problems every month → view 6.

steps.title: Quiz: the six components
steps.body: Practise the model.

quiz.question: A self-organised team is very motivated but is building a product nobody asked for. Which component of the model is missing?
options: Align constraints — clear purpose, goals and protection of shared resources
quiz.explanation: Self-organisation without direction can lead anywhere. Constraints and a clear goal are exactly the third component of the model.

steps.title: Quiz: choose the component
steps.body: One more.

quiz.question: The team has a clear goal and full authority, but the code quality is bad because nobody knows the new technology. Which component do you work on?
quiz.explanation: Authority and goals do not create skills. Competence development (training, pairing, coaching, discipline) is the manager's responsibility in the model.

steps.title: Practice: rate your team on six views
steps.body:
Take a team you know (yours, or one you observe) and give each of the six components a score from 1 to 5:

1. Energise people — are people motivated, creative, active?
2. Empower teams — do they have real authority and trust?
3. Align constraints — is the purpose clear? are shared resources protected?
4. Develop competence — do skills grow? is there discipline?
5. Grow structure — does information flow well? is the structure right?
6. Improve everything — is there regular reflection and change?

Find the LOWEST score — that is your first area of work. Write one small concrete action for it, with a date. This is the model in practical use.
keyPoints: Score 1–5 per component → work on the lowest
One small action with a date beats a big plan

steps.title: Chapter summary
steps.body:
The author's own summary of chapter 1 is worth keeping as a short reference.

• The human brain is built in such a way that it sees a definite cause behind every event. This tendency to establish causal links is useful for forecasting and planning. However, situations are often far more complex than they appear at first sight — and complexity theory says that using linear thinking to solve complex problems leads to painful mistakes.

• Although reductionism — understanding the nature of a system by analysing its components — has been very successful in science, it is now generally recognised that you can go too far along this path.

• To deal with many complex problems you need a more holistic approach, of the kind used for studying complex social systems: a whole-system view of the interactions taking place inside groups of people.

• Management 3.0 is a model of agile management that allows the approaches of complexity theory to be applied to the management of teams that develop software products using agile methods.

Everything else in the book — all six components — stands on these four statements.
keyPoints: Linear thinking on complex problems = painful mistakes
Reductionism is necessary but insufficient
Management 3.0 = complexity theory applied to agile teams
steps.example: Next time you hear «who is responsible for this failure?», you now have a complete answer path: check for the causality fallacy, look one level down, look at the system as a whole, then decide which of the six views to strengthen.

steps.title: Module summary
steps.body: The end of chapter 1.

quiz.question: Which sentence best summarises chapter 1?
options: Plans are useless, so do not plan
Managers should control everything even more carefully
Our brains simplify complex systems; we need holistic, complexity-based management — and that is what Management 3.0 offers
Agile methods solve all management problems
quiz.explanation: Chapter 1 is a diagnosis (linear thinking, reductionism, illusion of control) plus a proposed answer (the six-view model).

title: Chapter 2a · Where Agile came from
intro: The author's own first product, the birth of «light» methods, and the Agile Manifesto of 2001.

steps.title: A prelude: one developer, one product
steps.body:
Chapter 2 opens with a personal story that explains why the author believes in agile ideas.

In the early 1990s, while studying at Delft University of Technology, he wrote an accounting program in his free time — about 30 000 lines of code. He had no formal methodology, little experience of building software, and no manager, coach or mentor. What he did have: time, a computer, a vision and a strong desire to create something excellent.

To his own surprise, he managed to sell the program to a dozen customers, and some of them were pleasantly shocked that a software product could be simple, convenient and have a nice interface — for a 1990s program. Twenty years later he was still using it to manage his own finances.

How is that possible? How did an inexperienced programmer create a product of such quality that it worked almost flawlessly for two decades? «I have not the slightest idea», he writes. But he does have a list of points that any follower of agile methods will immediately recognise — and that list is the subject of the next step.
keyPoints: A student with no method built a product that lasted 20 years
No plan, no manager, no methodology — but strong motivation and discipline
The reasons behind it look strikingly agile
steps.example: Notice what is missing from the story: no requirements document, no Gantt chart, no estimation meetings. And yet the product outlived most enterprise software built with all of those.

steps.title: Why it worked (four agile signs)
steps.body:
The author's own explanation has four points.

1. HE WORKED WITH ENTHUSIASM. He had some experience of using accounting applications and was convinced they had been «designed in hell with the goal of taking away all vital energy from users». His vision was that his product would be completely different: using it would be a pleasure.

2. HE WAS HIS OWN DEMANDING CUSTOMER. He built the program for himself, not for others. He was happy to find buyers, but whatever he did, the most important thing was that the product worked exactly as HE wanted.

3. HE HAD NO PLAN — ONLY A LIST OF FEATURES. He started with the most frequently used operation: entering transactions. Then he moved to less critical functions such as balance reports and corrections. At the end he added optional pleasant things like hints and data export. He worked on it until he lost interest — and simply never declared the product finished.

4. THE PROCESS CHANGED WHILE HE WAS WRITING CODE. He began creating checklists for every procedure, and those lists gradually became longer. He had never heard of unit testing, but his system of checks and double-checks was no less reliable than the one pilots use.

Summary: motivation, a demanding customer, discipline and a self-organising process — and none of it required prior experience. What mattered was a passionate desire to learn.
keyPoints: Enthusiasm and a real (even internal) customer beat process
Feature list in priority order instead of a big plan
The process evolved with the product — and discipline was still there
steps.example: Translate the four points into a team: a vision people believe in, a real user in the room, a prioritised list instead of a fixed plan, and a process the team improves as it goes. That is more agile than any ceremony calendar.

steps.title: Quiz: what really mattered
steps.body: Read the story like an agile person.

quiz.question: Which of these was NOT among the reasons the author gives for his success?
options: He was highly motivated by his vision
He was his own demanding customer
He followed a detailed project plan from the start
His process evolved while he was building the product
quiz.explanation: There was no plan at all — only a list of features in priority order. This is exactly the agile pattern: value first, plan light, process emerging.

steps.title: The engineers built structure — too much of it
steps.body:
The author retells the history of software methods in a humorous «biblical» style: «In the beginning engineers created computers and software. The software was formless and non-functional, and darkness reigned over the users. And the engineers said: let there be structure. And structure appeared. Even too much of it.»

Over the last five or six decades many computer engineers worried about the unstable quality of software development. It was explained by the fact that different teams used different methods, mostly invented on the spot. So the engineers dived into work, and a number of FORMALISED approaches appeared. The profession of «software developer» was born. The starting hypothesis was that creating software is a purely ENGINEERING task.

The result was a large number of models, methods, approaches and techniques that were supposed to help programmers improve quality. But a strange thing happened: in most projects these methods turned out to be ineffective. Far more often the result was yet another bureaucracy. Software projects took so much time and required so much documentation that the «formal» requirements managed to change several times while the project was still in development.

Meanwhile small teams of programmers were releasing much better products much faster. Their advantages: enthusiasm, discipline, flexibility and methods adapted to each project. As the author puts it: «Evolution produced dinosaurs, but all the food went to the ants.»
keyPoints: Formal methods often produced bureaucracy, not quality
Requirements changed faster than heavy projects could deliver
Small adaptive teams won on speed and quality — «the ants got the food»
steps.example: A 200-page specification signed in January describes a product for a market that no longer exists in September. The document is perfect. The product is wrong. That is the dinosaur problem in one sentence.

steps.title: The «light» methods of the 1990s
steps.body:
In the early 1990s a new methodology appeared: RAPID APPLICATION DEVELOPMENT (RAD). Within it, the most successful development teams managed to combine some formalised methods borrowed from the «heavyweight» engineering approach (change control in technical documentation, inspections, use of metrics) with practice-driven methods such as prototyping, releasing incremental versions of software and close cooperation with the customer.

This crossing of formal and informal techniques produced the first «light» methodologies:
• Evolutionary project management (Evo) — 1988
• Scrum — 1995
• Dynamic systems development method (DSDM) — 1995
• Crystal — 1997
• Extreme Programming (XP) — 1999
• Feature-driven development (FDD) — 1999
• Pragmatic programming — 1999
• Adaptive software development — 2000

So many methods, articles, books and seminars about «light» methodologies appeared at once that some people compared it with the Cambrian explosion in biology — the moment when an enormous variety of life forms appeared in a geologically short time.
keyPoints: RAD mixed formal control with prototyping and customer cooperation
1988–2000 produced Evo, Scrum, DSDM, Crystal, XP, FDD and others
So much appeared at once that people called it a Cambrian explosion
steps.example: Notice the dates: most of these are older than many developers using them today. Scrum is from 1995 — the same year as the first version of Java.

steps.title: 2001: the Agile Manifesto
steps.body:
Because so many methods appeared at the same time, the leaders of the movement decided to meet and discuss the situation. In 2001 they gathered at a ski resort in Utah. There the term «agile methods» (Agile) was chosen, replacing the terminology used before, and the AGILE MANIFESTO of software development was created.

The four values, in the manifesto's own words:
• INDIVIDUALS AND INTERACTIONS over processes and tools
• WORKING SOFTWARE over comprehensive documentation
• CUSTOMER COLLABORATION over contract negotiation
• RESPONDING TO CHANGE over following a plan

And the crucial closing line: «That is, while there is value in the items on the right, we value the items on the left more.»

Many people saw the manifesto primarily as a reaction against the bureaucratic character of the formal approaches that existed at the time and were «too ordered». But few understood that the authors of the manifesto were also speaking out against the LACK OF DISCIPLINE among programmers, against «chaotic» processes and against the low quality that dominated the software market at that time.

The leaders of the new movement realised that there is a middle way between structure and the absence of structure, between order and chaos. In a certain sense it was a heroic attempt to return to an earlier era, when the main players were pioneer programmers — but without the anarchy.
keyPoints: Four values, always «X over Y», never «X instead of Y»
The right-hand items still have value — the left ones have more
Agile was a reaction against bureaucracy AND against chaos
steps.example: Two teams both say «we are agile». One has no tests, no definition of done and no plan. The other has short cycles, automated tests and a visible backlog. Only the second one matches what the manifesto's authors meant.

steps.title: Quiz: read the manifesto correctly
steps.body: A very common mistake.

quiz.question: «We value working software over comprehensive documentation» means…
options: Documentation is forbidden in agile teams
Documentation still has value, but working software has more value
Documentation should be written after the project
quiz.explanation: The manifesto says directly: the items on the right have value; we simply value the items on the left more. «Agile means no documents» is a myth.

steps.title: After the manifesto
steps.body:
Later the most authoritative representatives of the agile movement created the AGILE ALLIANCE — a non-profit organisation whose purpose is to promote agile methods worldwide.

A whole new ecosystem appeared, consisting of conferences, consultants, books and journals. As a result, software development processes became Agile with a capital A, turning into something deeper than just a set of practices you can use when building software.

Recognising that software development projects exist in the area located between order and chaos, agile approaches essentially became a way of life.

For this course that last sentence matters most. If development lives between order and chaos, then management must live there too — otherwise the two halves of the same organisation are playing different games. That is precisely the gap Management 3.0 tries to close.
keyPoints: Agile grew into a movement with its own ecosystem
Projects live between order and chaos — as a way of working, not a ritual
If development is agile and management is not, the two halves fight
steps.example: A company where developers work in two-week cycles while management demands a fixed twelve-month scope is not «half agile» — it is two systems fighting each other, and the friction shows up as endless replanning.

steps.title: Explain: what is Agile, in one minute
Module summary
steps.body: Fix chapter 2a.

quiz.question: What was the real innovation of the agile movement, according to the book?
options: Finding a middle way between heavy structure and chaos, with fast feedback and adaptation
Making projects cheaper by hiring fewer people
quiz.explanation: The leaders were against bureaucracy AND against undisciplined chaos. The middle way — with discipline, feedback and adaptation — is the core.

title: Chapter 2b · Seven dimensions of Agile
intro: The author's own short overview of agile fundamentals: people, functionality, quality, tools, time, value, process — plus a surprising eighth one.

steps.title: 1 · People
steps.body:
The author gives his own short overview of agile fundamentals through «seven dimensions» in which software projects live. The first is PEOPLE.

Agile methods recognise the uniqueness of people and do not treat them as interchangeable resources. It is also recognised that the main value lies in the interactions and cooperation between people, rather than in their individual competences.

This approach implies working in small CROSS-FUNCTIONAL teams that unite people performing different roles — developers, designers, testers and so on. The preferred option is for the team to sit in one room.

The team is required to SELF-ORGANISE, which means the absence of methods or work processes imposed from outside. The team is trusted to perform certain work, based on the idea that its members know how to do that work and are aware of their responsibility for the result.

For a manager this is a big shift. The job is no longer to distribute tasks among «resources», but to compose a team that is able to organise its own work — and then to protect the conditions that make that possible.
keyPoints: People are not interchangeable resources
Value lives in interaction and cooperation, not in individual skill
Small cross-functional teams that self-organise, ideally co-located
steps.example: «We need two more resources for Q3» versus «we need two people who know payments and can work with our team». The first sentence treats humans as units; the second is how agile teams are actually built.

steps.title: 2 · Functionality
steps.body:
Within agile methods it is recognised that the best software products are created when the CUSTOMER IS MAXIMALLY INVOLVED in the development process.

The team cooperates with the customer (or their representative), keeps the project backlog in an up-to-date state and constantly updates the shared priorities.

The description of the desired functionality is done in an extremely brief form and is detailed only immediately before work on it begins. This is the principle of late detail: writing detailed specifications for work that starts in six months is writing fiction, because priorities and understanding will change.

Simplicity is the key to good design of each functional capability. And the usefulness of that functionality is evaluated and confirmed by the client immediately after it has been created — not at the end of the project.

Together these two rules — DETAIL LATE, CONFIRM EARLY — remove most of the waste in requirements work.
keyPoints: Customer involvement is the strongest driver of product quality
Detail requirements late, confirm value early
Simplicity is the key to good design of every feature
steps.example: A team writes a one-line item: «customer can pay with a saved card». Three months later, when the work starts, they spend an hour detailing it with the customer — using everything they learned in those three months. Nothing was wasted on premature detail.

steps.title: 3 · Quality
keyPoints: Technical excellence is central, not optional
TDD, review/pairing, Definition of Done, refactoring, emerging architecture
Flexible plan + strict quality = agile; flexible quality = chaos
steps.example: «Let's skip tests this sprint, we're in a hurry» is not an agile trade-off. In agile the variable you cut is SCOPE — you ship fewer features at the same quality, because quality is what keeps you fast next month.

steps.title: Quiz: quality myth
steps.body: A very common misunderstanding.

quiz.question: «We are agile, so we have no time for tests and refactoring.» What is wrong with this sentence?
