options: Nothing, speed is the point of Agile
Agile puts technical excellence in the centre: TDD, reviews, Definition of Done and refactoring are part of the method, not extras
Tests are only needed in waterfall projects
Refactoring should be done once a year
quiz.explanation: The flexible part is the PLAN, not the quality. Skipping quality practices is not Agile — it is just chaos with a nice name.

steps.title: 4 · Tools
steps.body:
Supporters of agile methods consider TOOLS the least important factor influencing the success of a project. And nevertheless tools are often mentioned and promoted in the literature on agile methodologies.

Experienced agile teams prefer tools that allow daily builds, continuous integration and automated testing. Teams need motivation, so repeating boring operations must be automated — machines do not get bored, people do.

Many supporters of flexible methodologies put forward as a mandatory condition the presence of a supporting «habitat» in the form of an open office space, as well as information radiators — for example a task board and burndown charts.

The purpose of tools in the context of agile methods is formulated very clearly: to strengthen MOTIVATION, COMMUNICATION and COOPERATION inside the team. Any tool that increases control but decreases those three is working against the method, whatever its marketing says.
keyPoints: Tools are the least important success factor
Automate the boring and repetitive — that is what tools are for
Purpose: motivation, communication, cooperation — not control
steps.example: A task board on a wall that everyone sees while drinking coffee often beats an expensive tracker nobody opens. The question is never «is the tool powerful?» but «does it help us talk and stay motivated?»

steps.title: 5 · Time
steps.body:
Agile methods have a special relationship with TIME. In agile projects, delivery dates, budgets and deadlines can be set almost arbitrarily.

Software is created in short segments, often within timeboxes or «sprints», and is delivered in the form of incremental releases — where each release is itself potentially a product ready for delivery.

This allows business owners to manage the project schedule, moving the date of the finished product forward or backward depending on when they want to make one or another piece of functionality available.

Meanwhile the team strives to find for itself the optimal speed of development — one that it can maintain practically indefinitely. This is the idea of sustainable pace: not the maximum speed for two months followed by burnout, but the speed you can keep for years.

The combination is powerful: the business controls WHAT is released and WHEN, while the team controls HOW MUCH fits into a healthy pace.
keyPoints: Short timeboxes; every increment potentially shippable
Business steers the release date by choosing scope
Sustainable pace: a speed the team can keep almost indefinitely
steps.example: «We can ship on 15 March» becomes «on 15 March you will have whatever is finished by then — and here is the ordered list, so you choose what is at the top». Same date, honest content.

steps.title: 6 · Value
steps.body:
One of the most important reasons for creating the Agile Manifesto was the desire to emphasise the importance of TIMELY REACTION TO CHANGE.

The environment in which a software product functions is never static. Functionality that yesterday represented significant value may turn out to be useless tomorrow — INCLUDING functionality that already exists in versions of the product delivered to the customer. This last point is easy to forget: value can evaporate from features you already shipped.

Developers who practise flexible methodologies try to cope with this problem by preferring short cycles of development and feedback. The meaning of frequent releases of a software product is not only to get feedback from users and take it into account in further development, but also to give users new functionality as soon as possible after their need for it has been identified — thereby increasing the value of the software for the client.

So «value» in agile is not a slogan: it is a scheduling principle. Ship earlier, learn earlier, adjust earlier.
keyPoints: Value changes over time — even in features already delivered
Short development and feedback cycles are the answer
Frequent releases = feedback + faster value for the client
steps.example: A feature planned in January as «critical» becomes irrelevant in May because a competitor changed the market. A team that ships monthly notices in February. A team that ships yearly finds out after it is built.

steps.title: 7 · Process
keyPoints: Rolling-wave planning, daily talk, retrospectives
Progress = working software accepted by the client
Light process, but a real and disciplined one
steps.example: «We are 80% done» has meant nothing for decades. «Users can register, log in and pay; refunds are not implemented yet» means everything — and it is checkable.

steps.title: 8 · Conflict (the bonus dimension)
steps.body:
The author ends the overview honestly. Everything described above reflects HIS understanding of the essence of agile methods. Naturally, this is no more than his point of view, and some developers practising flexible methodologies may disagree with his brief description.

But, he says, this follows from the very character of agile methods. He could even include the concept of CONFLICT as an eighth dimension inherent to these methodologies.

As the book shows later, the presence of internal conflict is a natural property of complex systems and a necessary condition for creativity and innovation. Systems without any internal tension do not adapt and do not invent — they only repeat.

And he closes with a sentence worth remembering: «It is a great honour to be among people for whom nothing brings so much pleasure as the opportunity to improve each other.»

For a manager the practical consequence is uncomfortable but useful: a team where nobody ever disagrees is not a healthy team. It is a team where disagreement has become unsafe.
keyPoints: Conflict is natural in complex systems and needed for innovation
Zero disagreement is a warning sign, not harmony
Improving each other is a feature of strong teams, not a threat
steps.example: In a healthy team a junior can say «I think this design will not scale» and get a real discussion. In a silent team the same thought appears six months later in an exit interview.

steps.title: Quiz: the seven dimensions
steps.body: Practise the map.

quiz.question: A team releases every two weeks, but only shows slides about progress instead of working software. Which dimension is broken?
options: Process — progress must be measured by working software accepted by the client
quiz.explanation: Monitoring progress through working functionality is one of the key agile processes. Slides can hide the real state for months.

steps.title: Practice: score your project on 7 dimensions
steps.body:
Take a real project (work, study, a personal product) and give a score 1–5 for each dimension:

1. People — small cross-functional team, self-organising?
2. Functionality — real customer involved, detail added late, value confirmed early?
3. Quality — tests, reviews, Definition of Done, refactoring?
4. Tools — do they help communication and motivation, or create noise?
5. Time — short cycles, sustainable pace?
6. Value — fast feedback, frequent releases?
7. Process — light planning, daily talk, retrospectives?

Then: choose the two lowest and write one small improvement for each, with a date. Add a personal question: how does our team handle CONFLICT — do people say what they really think?
keyPoints: Score 7 dimensions → pick 2 weakest → one small action each

steps.title: Module summary
steps.body: Fix the fundamentals.

quiz.question: Which sentence matches the book's view of agile fundamentals?
options: Agile is a fixed set of practices that all teams must follow
Agile is a set of principles across several dimensions (people, functionality, quality, tools, time, value, process) that each team adapts — including healthy conflict
Agile is only about short sprints
Agile means the customer decides everything
quiz.explanation: The author gives dimensions, not rules — exactly matching the descriptive approach of the whole book.

title: Chapter 2c · Methods that compete with Agile
intro: Lean software development, software craftsmanship — and why healthy competition between methods is a good sign.

steps.title: Competition is normal and healthy
steps.body:
«Rarely do we come across games that do not involve competition between players, and few systems manage without conflict. Without differences in views between people, life would be less interesting.»

Fortunately, in the world of flexible technologies there is enough healthy competition: between Scrum and Extreme Programming, between Scrum and Kanban, and even between Scrum and Scrum — there are different schools inside the same method.

But agile methods are not the only players in this field. There exist several strong and promising competing approaches. Some of them are based on ideas analogous to agile methods, some complement them, and some enter into direct contradiction with them.

For a manager the practical conclusion is toolbox thinking: stop asking «which method is the true one?» and start asking «which idea fits this problem, this team and this moment?» The book itself is built on exactly this attitude — it offers understanding, and expects you to assemble your own recipe.
keyPoints: Healthy competition between methods is a sign of a living field
Some approaches complement Agile, some contradict it
Toolbox thinking: match the idea to the problem, not to your identity
steps.example: A team with a stable flow of small requests may be better served by Kanban than by sprints. Insisting on Scrum because «we are an agile company» is method-worship, not agility.

steps.title: Lean software development
steps.body:
One of the biggest competitors are the methodologies of LEAN SOFTWARE DEVELOPMENT, which transfer the ideas of lean manufacturing into the area of software creation.

The seven principles of lean production are based on the fourteen principles of the Toyota Way (the management philosophy of the Toyota company) and the fourteen management principles of W. Edwards Deming.

There is a lot in common between agile and lean methodologies, so they often play on the same side. The same experts work with both, they have the same fans, and their development is covered in the same blogs, journals and TV shows.

From the management point of view, lean methodologies — with their emphasis on REDUCING UNPRODUCTIVE COSTS (waste) and OPTIMISING SYSTEMS AS A WHOLE — made a big contribution to the development of flexible methodologies. And although lean software development appeared several years later than Agile, it became comparable with it in the number of consultants, coaches, professional consortiums and conferences held.

The two lean ideas most useful for a manager are exactly those two: see the waste, and optimise the whole rather than the parts.
keyPoints: Lean = Toyota Way + Deming applied to software
Its two gifts: reduce waste, optimise the whole system
Agile and Lean usually play on the same side
steps.example: A feature sits «done by development» for three weeks waiting for QA, then two more waiting for release. The coding took four days. Lean makes you look at those five weeks of waiting — the part nobody was measuring.

steps.title: Software craftsmanship
steps.body:
A smaller but very capable player is the movement for SOFTWARE CRAFTSMANSHIP.

Its central idea: writing software is a craft, and a developer should grow like a craftsman — through deliberate practice, mentoring and personal responsibility for the quality of the work. The focus is on the professional standards of the individual developer, not only on the process of the team.

Why this matters for a manager: agile processes ASSUME technical excellence but do not teach it. Scrum will not make anyone write better code; retrospectives will not turn a junior into a senior. Craftsmanship fills exactly that gap — it is about how people actually become good at the work itself.

(Here the preview edition of the book ends. The full version continues with complexity theory in chapter 3, and then with the six components of Management 3.0, two chapters each.)

So the final picture of chapter 2 is a landscape rather than a single road: agile methods, lean thinking and craftsmanship — three complementary answers to the same problem of building good software in a complex world.
keyPoints: Craftsmanship = mastery, mentoring, personal professional standards
Process assumes skill; craftsmanship builds it
Agile + Lean + Craftsmanship: three complementary answers
steps.example: A team adopts Scrum and quality does not improve. They add pairing, code kata sessions and a mentoring pair for each junior — and six months later the bug rate halves. The process was never the missing part; the craft was.

steps.title: Quiz: which approach helps?
steps.body: Use the toolbox.

quiz.question: Your team has good sprints, but a lot of work is wasted: half-finished features wait for weeks between stages. Which approach addresses this most directly?
options: Lean thinking: reduce waste and optimise the flow of the whole system
quiz.explanation: Waiting work between stages is classic waste. Lean focuses on flow and on optimising the system as a whole, not single steps.

steps.title: Quiz: the other one
steps.body: And the second case.

quiz.question: The process is fine, but the code is fragile and juniors have nobody to learn from. Which movement is most relevant?
options: Software craftsmanship: mastery, mentoring, professional standards
quiz.explanation: Process does not create skill. Craftsmanship works exactly on how people become excellent at the craft itself.

steps.title: Practice: build your own toolbox
steps.body:
Write a short personal note (5–7 lines):

1. Which approach fits my current context best right now — Agile practices, Lean flow thinking, or craftsmanship? Why?
2. Which ONE idea from the other two do I want to borrow?
3. What is the first small step to try it (this week or next)?

This matches the philosophy of the whole book: no single method is «the truth». You take the ideas that fit your situation and build your own recipe.
keyPoints: Pick a base, borrow from others, test in small steps

steps.title: Module summary
steps.body: Fix chapter 2c.

quiz.question: What is the author's attitude to competing methods?
options: Agile is the only right way
Competition and conflict between approaches are healthy; borrow ideas that fit your context
Choose one method and never change it
quiz.explanation: This matches both the pragmatist position and complexity thinking: many partial models, no single perfect one.

title: Drill · Quiz marathon
intro: Mixed questions from the whole course. Do 6–8 at a time.

steps.title: M1
steps.body: Basics.

quiz.question: «All organisations are networks» means…
options: In practice work and information flow through relationships, even when the org chart shows a hierarchy
quiz.explanation: The chart is the map; the network is the territory. Authority still flows through hierarchy — but communication flows through the network.

steps.title: M2
steps.body: Basics.

quiz.question: What is the pragmatist position on self-organisation?
options: It always gives the best result
It is powerful, but it needs direction and someone responsible for the result — it has no value in itself
quiz.explanation: This is the position between princes and priests: teams organise the work, but goals and constraints come from those responsible to the owners.

steps.title: M3
steps.body: Versions.

quiz.question: A company adds OKRs, engagement surveys and a leadership academy — but all decisions still come from the top. Version?
quiz.explanation: Add-ons on top of an unchanged top-down architecture is the definition of 2.0.

steps.title: M4
steps.body: Complexity.

quiz.question: Which statement about complexity is TRUE?
options: Complexity always means very many elements
Three elements can already produce complex behaviour
quiz.explanation: The water molecule and the three-body problem are the book's examples: complexity is about interaction, not quantity.

steps.title: M5
steps.body: Complexity.

quiz.question: Your plan for a complex project keeps failing. The book's explanation is…
options: Complex systems cannot be predicted in detail; the answer is short cycles, experiments and adaptation
You need a longer planning phase
quiz.explanation: Deterministic calculation is the wrong tool for complex systems — no matter how good you are at using it.

steps.title: M6
steps.body: Linear thinking.

quiz.question: Which sentence shows the causality fallacy?
options: «There were several factors, and they influenced each other»
«The release was late because of the new tester»
«We do not know the cause yet»
«Let's run an experiment to find out»
quiz.explanation: One convenient cause and one guilty person for a complex outcome — a classic example.

steps.title: M7
steps.body: Control.

quiz.question: Why do old control systems fail in product development?
options: They work only for repeated operations that need no thinking; creative work needs different approaches
They were invented too long ago
quiz.explanation: The author is precise here: control is effective for repetitive work. The mistake is applying it to creative work.

steps.title: M8
steps.body: Reductionism.

quiz.question: The mechanical duck picture illustrates…
options: Reductionism that went too far: you cannot find «walking» or «quacking» in the separate parts
quiz.explanation: It is the book's visual joke about the limits of taking systems apart.

steps.title: M9
steps.body: Levels.

quiz.question: Hierarchical reductionism says you should explain a level…
options: By the level exactly one step below
quiz.explanation: Dawkins's compromise: one level down. So a team is explained by people and relations — not by neurons or quarks.

steps.title: M10
steps.body: Leaky abstractions.

quiz.question: «The law of leaky abstractions» in management means…
options: Problems from lower levels break through into higher levels, so leaders still need people and communication skills
quiz.explanation: Delegation is fine — but leaks happen, and then you need the skills you thought you delegated away.

steps.title: M11
steps.body: The model.

quiz.question: Which is NOT one of the six views of Management 3.0?
quiz.explanation: «Utilisation of resources» is exactly the old 1.0 language. The six views are: energise, empower, align constraints, develop competence, grow structure, improve everything.

steps.title: M12
steps.body: The model.

quiz.question: Team members are skilled and motivated, and they have authority — but two teams keep building the same thing twice. Which view needs work?
options: Grow structure — communication and information flow between teams
quiz.explanation: Duplicated work is usually a structure and communication problem, not a skill or motivation problem.

steps.title: M13
steps.body: Agile history.

quiz.question: What did the 2001 meeting in Utah produce?
options: The term «Agile» and the Agile Manifesto
quiz.explanation: The methods existed before (Scrum 1995, XP 1999); in 2001 the leaders chose a common name and wrote the manifesto.

steps.title: M14
steps.body: Manifesto.

quiz.question: Which pair is NOT one of the four manifesto values?
options: Individuals and interactions over processes and tools
Responding to change over following a plan
quiz.explanation: Speed over quality is not in the manifesto. In fact the movement was also a reaction against low quality and chaos.

steps.title: M15
steps.body: Dimensions.

quiz.question: «Detail the requirement only just before you start working on it» belongs to which dimension?
quiz.explanation: Late detail and early confirmation of value are core parts of the functionality dimension.

steps.title: M16
steps.body: Dimensions.

quiz.question: Which practice belongs to the QUALITY dimension?
quiz.explanation: Definition of Done sits with TDD, code review and refactoring in the technical excellence group.

steps.title: M17
steps.body: Dimensions.

quiz.question: «Sustainable pace» belongs to…
quiz.explanation: The time dimension: short cycles, incremental releases, and a speed the team can keep almost indefinitely.

steps.title: M18
steps.body: Tools.

quiz.question: What is the purpose of tools in the agile context?
options: To strengthen motivation, communication and cooperation inside the team
quiz.explanation: Tools are the least important success factor — and their job is to help the team, not to watch it.

steps.title: M19
steps.body: Conflict.

quiz.question: Why does the author call conflict a possible eighth dimension of Agile?
options: Because agile teams argue a lot
Because internal conflict is natural in complex systems and necessary for creativity and innovation
It was a joke with no meaning
quiz.explanation: «It is a great honour to be among people who enjoy improving each other.» A team with no disagreement is usually a silent team.

steps.title: M20
steps.body: Competitors.

quiz.question: Lean software development is based on…
options: The Toyota Way and Deming's management principles
quiz.explanation: Seven lean principles built on fourteen Toyota Way principles and fourteen Deming principles.

steps.title: M21
steps.body: Mixed.

quiz.question: Which action fits Management 3.0 best?
options: Write a detailed two-year plan and follow it strictly
Give the team a clear goal and constraints, then let them decide how to work — and check the working result often
Assign every task personally each morning
Measure lines of code per developer
quiz.explanation: Clear direction plus autonomy plus fast feedback: align constraints + empower teams + improve everything.

steps.title: M22
steps.body: Mixed.

quiz.question: A manager says: «If people self-organise, I have nothing to do.» What is the correct answer?
options: True, agile teams need no managers
The manager's job changes: energising people, setting constraints and goals, growing competence and structure, driving improvement
The manager should become a developer
The manager should control the sprint backlog
quiz.explanation: The six views are exactly a job description for a manager in an agile organisation.

steps.title: M23
steps.body: Mixed.

quiz.question: What does «descriptive, not normative» mean for you as a reader?
options: You must follow the book's rules exactly
You get understanding of how systems behave and build your own practices for your context
The book has no useful content
You should only read the theory chapters
quiz.explanation: This is the author's main promise — and the reason there are no case studies or checklists.

steps.title: M24 · Final
steps.body: The whole course in one question.

quiz.question: Summarise the course in one sentence:
options: «Use Scrum and everything will be fine»
«Organisations are complex living networks; a manager's job is to energise people, empower teams, align constraints, develop competence, grow structure and improve everything»
«Managers are obstacles and should be removed»
quiz.explanation: Complexity as the foundation, six views as the job description. Marathon complete! 🏁

title: Drill · Real work situations
intro: Apply the model to everyday management situations. Choose the answer that matches Management 3.0.

steps.title: S1: the estimate
steps.body: Situation.

quiz.question: Your manager asks for an exact date for a feature that nobody has built before. Best answer?
options: Give a confident date to look professional
Say it is impossible to know anything
Give a range plus a plan to reduce uncertainty: «two to five weeks; after a two-day spike we can narrow it down»
quiz.explanation: Complexity does not mean «no answer». It means honest ranges plus cheap experiments that reduce uncertainty.

steps.title: S2: the late project
steps.body: Situation.

quiz.question: A project is late. The director asks: «Who is responsible?» A Management 3.0 answer would be…
options: «Let's look at the system: dependencies, unclear goals, interruptions — there are usually several causes that reinforce each other»
quiz.explanation: Single-cause thinking is the causality fallacy. Systemic causes usually explain more — and are actually fixable.

steps.title: S3: micro-management
steps.body: Situation.

quiz.question: A manager checks every task in the tracker twice a day and re-assigns work. Which two views does this damage most?
quiz.explanation: Removing authority destroys empowerment, and constant control destroys motivation. The intention may be good; the effect is not.

steps.title: S4: the silent team
steps.body: Situation.

quiz.question: In retrospectives everyone says «everything is fine» for three months. What does the book suggest you think?
options: Zero disagreement is a warning sign: conflict is natural and necessary — people probably do not feel safe to speak
quiz.explanation: Conflict is the possible «eighth dimension» — its total absence usually means silence, not harmony.

steps.title: S5: the new tool
steps.body: Situation.

quiz.question: Management buys an expensive tool to «make the team agile». What is wrong?
options: Tools are the least important success factor; agility comes from people, feedback and process — a tool cannot create it
The team should have chosen a different vendor
quiz.explanation: Tools should support motivation and communication. They cannot replace them.

steps.title: S6: two teams, one goal
steps.body: Situation.

quiz.question: Two teams optimise their own metrics and the product as a whole gets worse. Which idea explains this best?
options: Local optimisation: improving parts does not improve the whole — you need whole-system thinking (a lean idea, and pure complexity thinking)
quiz.explanation: This is the practical version of «the system is not the sum of its parts».

steps.title: S7: the star developer
steps.body: Situation.

quiz.question: One brilliant developer writes most of the code but shares nothing. Which views should the manager work on?
options: Develop competence (mentoring, pairing) and grow structure (information flow) — plus align constraints so knowledge sharing is part of «done»
quiz.explanation: A single point of knowledge is a systemic risk. It is fixed by structure and competence work, not by praise or blame.

steps.title: S8: the reorganisation
steps.body: Situation.

quiz.question: Top management announces a big reorganisation designed in detail by consultants, to start on one date. What does the book predict?
options: It will work if the design is good enough
Detailed top-down design of a complex social system usually fails; small changes with feedback work better
It will work if people are motivated
quiz.explanation: This is the illusion of design from above — the same mistake as the author's 30-page business plan, but at organisational scale.

steps.title: S9: quality pressure
steps.body: Situation.

quiz.question: The deadline is close. The manager suggests: «skip the tests this sprint». A good agile answer:
options: «Then let's cut SCOPE instead: quality practices are what keep our speed. Which features can move to the next release?»
quiz.explanation: In agile the flexible variable is scope, not quality. Skipping quality borrows speed today and pays it back with interest.

steps.title: S10: remote team
steps.body: Situation.

quiz.question: A distributed team communicates only in tickets, and misunderstandings grow. Which view is weakest?
options: Grow structure — the communication structure does not fit the work
quiz.explanation: Structure is about how information flows. If the channel does not fit the complexity of the topic, you get misunderstandings — not lazy people.

steps.title: S11: bonuses
steps.body: Situation.

quiz.question: The company introduces individual bonuses for the number of closed tickets. What does the book's view predict?
options: People will optimise the metric, not the value: smaller tickets, less helping others, worse teamwork
quiz.explanation: Broken incentive systems are one of the book's examples of Management 1.0 damage — including their role in the financial crisis.

steps.title: S12: «we are agile»
steps.body: Situation.

quiz.question: A team has stand-ups and sprints, but the boss decides everything and there is no feedback from users. Is this agile?
options: No: without autonomy and real feedback loops the ceremonies are 1.0 management in agile clothes
Yes, if sprints are two weeks
quiz.explanation: Ceremonies are not the point. Autonomy, working software and short feedback cycles are.

steps.title: Practice: your own case
steps.body:
Take a real difficult situation from your work or study group and analyse it as a complex system:

1. Write the situation in three lines, facts only.
2. List at least THREE possible causes (not one!). Mark which of them could reinforce each other.
3. Which of the six views is weakest here: energise / empower / align / develop / grow / improve?
4. Design one small EXPERIMENT (not a big plan) to test one cause — something you can do in a week.
5. Decide how you will know whether it helped.

This is the whole book in one exercise: multiple causes, systemic view, small safe experiment, feedback.
keyPoints: 3+ causes, not one
One weakest view + one week-sized experiment + a way to measure

title: Glossary · Key terms
intro: Short definitions of all the important terms of the course, for quick review.

steps.title: Terms: management versions
steps.body:
• MANAGEMENT 1.0 — top-down hierarchy, command and control; power in few hands.
• MANAGEMENT 2.0 — the same hierarchy plus add-ons (Six Sigma, scorecards, advice books). Cosmetic, not structural.
• MANAGEMENT 3.0 — management based on complexity theory: organisations are living networks; the manager works with people, constraints and conditions.
• PRINCES — top managers who claim leadership by title.
• PRIESTS — people who claim management is unnecessary.
• PRAGMATISTS — the book's position: hierarchy for authority, networks for communication.
keyPoints: 1.0 hierarchy → 2.0 add-ons → 3.0 networks
Communication through networks, authority through hierarchy

steps.title: Terms: complexity
steps.body:
• DETERMINISM — future events follow from past events by natural laws; predictable in principle.
• COMPLEXITY — behaviour that cannot be predicted from the parts; not about big numbers (three elements are enough).
• LINEAR THINKING — expecting simple causes and simple effects.
• CAUSALITY FALLACY — assuming one cause (and often one guilty person) for a complex outcome.
• REDUCTIONISM — understanding a system by studying its parts.
• GREEDY REDUCTIONISM — trying to explain everything by the smallest parts.
• HIERARCHICAL REDUCTIONISM — explaining a level by the level exactly one step below.
• HOLISM — the behaviour of the whole is not the sum of its parts.
• LEAKY ABSTRACTION — problems from lower levels breaking into higher levels.
keyPoints: Complexity ≠ many parts
Explain one level down; expect leaks

steps.title: Terms: the model
steps.body:
The six views of Management 3.0:

1. ENERGISE PEOPLE — keep people active, creative and motivated.
2. EMPOWER TEAMS — give real authority and trust so teams can self-organise.
3. ALIGN CONSTRAINTS — give clear purpose and goals; protect people and shared resources.
4. DEVELOP COMPETENCE — grow skills and discipline so teams can reach the goals.
5. GROW STRUCTURE — build the social/communication structure that lets information flow.
6. IMPROVE EVERYTHING — continuous improvement of people, teams and organisation.

Memory hook: energise → empower → align → develop → grow → improve.
keyPoints: Six words = a manager's job description in an agile company

steps.title: Terms: agile fundamentals
steps.body:
The seven dimensions (plus one):

• PEOPLE — small cross-functional self-organising teams; people are not interchangeable.
• FUNCTIONALITY — customer involved, backlog, late detail, early confirmation, simplicity.
• QUALITY — TDD, code review, pair programming, Definition of Done, refactoring, gradual design.
• TOOLS — least important; support builds, CI, automated tests, information radiators.
• TIME — timeboxes/sprints, incremental potentially shippable releases, sustainable pace.
• VALUE — value changes; short cycles; frequent releases for feedback and faster benefit.
• PROCESS — minimal (rolling-wave) planning, daily communication, progress by working software, retrospectives.
• CONFLICT (bonus) — natural in complex systems and necessary for creativity.
keyPoints: Seven dimensions describe Agile better than any single method

steps.title: Glossary check 1
steps.body: Quick recall.

quiz.question: «Explain a level by the level exactly one step below» is…
quiz.explanation: Dawkins's compromise between full reductionism and holism.

steps.title: Glossary check 2
steps.body: Quick recall.

quiz.question: Which view covers «clear purpose, goals, and protection of shared resources»?
quiz.explanation: Self-organisation can go anywhere — constraints give it direction and safety.

steps.title: Glossary check 3
steps.body: Quick recall.

quiz.question: Which is a QUALITY practice, not a PROCESS practice?
quiz.explanation: Refactoring belongs to technical excellence; the other three are process practices.

steps.title: Practice: draw the map from memory
steps.body:
Without looking, draw a one-page map of the course:

• centre: «Management 3.0»
• branch 1: three versions of management (1.0 / 2.0 / 3.0)
• branch 2: complexity ideas (determinism, complexity, linear thinking, reductionism, holism, leaky abstractions)
• branch 3: the six views
• branch 4: agile dimensions (seven + conflict)
• branch 5: competing approaches (Lean, craftsmanship)

Then compare with the glossary steps. What did you forget? That is your review list.
keyPoints: Recalling from memory fixes knowledge far better than re-reading

title: Practice · 14 days of small experiments
intro: One small action per day: turn the theory into working habits. Each step = one day, 10–20 minutes.

steps.title: How this practicum works
steps.body:
Rules for the next two weeks:

• One step per day, 10–20 minutes.
• Use REAL material: your work, your team, your project, your study group.
• Write short notes (3–5 lines per day). Without writing, the brain counts «I thought about it» as «I did it».
• If you miss a day, just continue — no guilt.

Week 1 is about seeing systems and causes. Week 2 is about acting like a Management 3.0 manager: constraints, empowerment, feedback and improvement.
keyPoints: One small action per day + 3–5 lines of notes

steps.title: Day 1 · Map the real network
steps.body:
Draw two pictures of your team or organisation:

1. The official hierarchy (boxes and lines from the org chart).
2. The REAL network: who talks to whom to get work done. Draw the actual paths — including group chats, informal advisors, «the person who really knows how it works».

Compare. Where are the biggest differences? Who is a network hub with no formal power?

steps.title: Day 2 · Three causes instead of one
steps.body:
Take one problem from this week that people explained with a single cause («X happened because of Y»).

Write at least THREE plausible causes. Mark the ones that could reinforce each other (circular effects).

Question for your notes: would all involved people agree with your original single explanation?

steps.title: Day 3 · Calculation or experiment
steps.body:
List five things you are currently trying to plan or predict.

Mark each: [C] can be calculated / [E] can only be tried and observed.

For one [E] item, design a cheap experiment for this week instead of a detailed plan. Write what result would change your mind.

steps.title: Day 4 · Catch a leaky abstraction
steps.body:
Find one place where a low-level detail broke something at a high level (a small bug that became a client problem, one unclear form that stopped a plan).

Write: the low-level cause → how it leaked upwards → one change that would make the higher level more robust.

steps.title: Day 5 · Score the six views
steps.body:
Score your team 1–5 on: energise people, empower teams, align constraints, develop competence, grow structure, improve everything.

Write one sentence of evidence for each score (not a feeling — an example). Circle the lowest score.

steps.title: Day 6 · One constraint, clearly stated
steps.body:
Take the goal your team is working on now and write it as a Management 3.0 constraint set:

• Purpose: why this matters (one sentence)
• Goal: what «good» looks like, measurable if possible
• Boundaries: what must NOT be broken (budget, quality, security, users)
• Free space: what the team decides completely on its own

If you cannot fill the last line — that is the real finding of today.

steps.title: Day 7 · Week review
steps.body:
Read your notes from days 1–6 and answer:

1. What surprised me most?
2. Where did I catch myself in linear thinking?
3. Which view (of six) is really the weakest — and what evidence do I have?

Write one sentence about what you want to change in week 2.

steps.title: Day 8 · Give away one decision
steps.body:
Find one decision you (or your manager) usually make, which the team could make instead.

Give it away explicitly: say what the boundaries are, and that inside them the decision is theirs. Write down what you fear might happen — and check the reality in a few days.

steps.title: Day 9 · Ask instead of telling
steps.body:
For one day, in every work conversation where you would normally give an answer, ask a question first: «what do you think we should do?», «what options do you see?»

Count how many times the answer you received was as good as yours or better. Write the number in your notes.

steps.title: Day 10 · Shorten one feedback loop
steps.body:
Find the longest feedback loop in your work (weeks between doing something and learning whether it was right).

Cut it in half with one concrete change: a demo mid-sprint, a five-user test, an early draft sent to the client, a smaller release.

Write the change and the date you will try it.

steps.title: Day 11 · Make information flow
steps.body:
Pick one piece of information that people repeatedly ask you for (status, priorities, who does what).

Make it visible instead: a shared board, a pinned message, a simple dashboard, a weekly two-line update.

This is «grow structure» in its smallest practical form.

steps.title: Day 12 · Competence, one small step
steps.body:
Choose one skill gap in your team (or in yourself).

Design the smallest possible development step: 30 minutes of pairing, one internal demo, one article read together, one code review with explanations.

Schedule it — a date, not «someday».

steps.title: Day 13 · Improve the process itself
steps.body:
Run a mini-retrospective (alone or with the team), 15 minutes:

• What worked well in the last two weeks?
• What slowed us down?
• ONE change we will try in the next two weeks.

Write the one change down and name the person who will start it (it can be you).

steps.title: Day 14 · Final review
steps.body:
Close the practicum:

1. Three things I now see differently about my team or work.
2. Which experiments actually changed something — and which did not?
3. My personal management principles (3–5 lines, in my own words).
4. My next month: one habit I keep from these 14 days.

Congratulations — you turned a management book into practice. That is what the author asked for in every «Reflect and act» section. 🎉
keyPoints: Keep one habit, not ten

title: Final · Your management system
intro: Put everything together: what you learned, what to remember in a year, and how to keep growing.

steps.title: What you now have
keyPoints: Systems view + six views + agile dimensions + toolbox thinking

steps.title: Write your one-page cheat sheet
steps.body:
Create a one-page note you will actually keep:

1. Six views with one question each («Are people energised?», «Do teams have real authority?»…).
2. Two complexity reminders: «what is calculable here, what must be tried?» and «what are three possible causes?».
3. Your favourite manifesto line, in your own words.
4. Your personal red flags (micro-management, single-cause stories, ceremonies without feedback…).
5. Your monthly ritual: score the six views, pick the weakest, run one experiment.

Keep it where you plan your week.
keyPoints: Six questions + two reminders + red flags + a monthly ritual

steps.title: How to continue
steps.body:
This edition of the book covers chapter 1 and the beginning of chapter 2. If you want to go further, the full book continues with:

• Chapter 3 — complexity theory in more depth (the scientific base of the whole model).
• Chapters 4–5 — energise people (motivation in theory and practice).
• Chapters 6–7 — empower teams (authority, delegation, trust).
• Chapters 8–9 — align constraints (purpose, goals, protecting resources).
• Chapters 10–11 — develop competence (skills, discipline, the seven dimensions again).
• Chapters 12–13 — grow structure (organisational and social-network design).
• Chapters 14–15 — improve everything (continuous improvement, change management).
• Chapter 16 — «All models are wrong, but some are useful».

Also useful: the companion site management30.com with extra materials.
keyPoints: The full book: six components × 2 chapters + conclusions

steps.title: Teach it to someone
steps.body:
The best way to finish: explain the core of this course to another person in about three minutes.

Structure you can use:
1. Why old management fails with modern work (complexity, linear thinking).
2. What changes in Management 3.0 (networks, living systems).
3. The six views as a manager's job.
4. One example from your own experience.

If you can do this without notes, the material is yours.

steps.title: Graduation 🎓
steps.body: The last question of the course.

quiz.question: In a year, what is the ONE thing you should still remember from this book?
options: The names of all agile methods from the 1990s
That teams are complex living systems: give people energy, teams authority, work clear constraints, grow skills and structure — and improve continuously with fast feedback
quiz.explanation: Terms fade; the systems view and the six views stay. Course complete — well done! 🏆
